hints: Notice there are two separate liquid layers with different depths and densities: 9.0 cm of $1000 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$ water and 5.0 cm of $800 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$ oil.
Recall hydrostatic pressure for each layer is $p = h\rho g$, so you need two pressures with depths converted from cm to m.
Calculate the water pressure and the oil pressure separately, then add them because both layers press on the base.
walkthrough: Convert depths to metres: water $h_w = 9.0 \text{ cm} = 0.090 \text{ m}$ and oil $h_o = 5.0 \text{ cm} = 0.050 \text{ m}$.
State the hydrostatic pressure rule $p = h\rho g$ with $g \approx 9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$ and apply it to each liquid separately.
Add the contributions because the base supports the weight of both liquids: $p_{total} = p_w + p_o \approx 883 + 392 \approx 1275 \text{ Pa}$.
Round to two significant figures as in the data, about $1300 \text{ Pa}$. This is option D.

options.A: This is the pressure due to the 5.0 cm of oil alone, $p = 0.050 \times 800 \times 9.81 \approx 390 \text{ Pa}$, not the total of oil plus water.
options.B: This is the pressure due to the 9.0 cm of water alone, $p = 0.090 \times 1000 \times 9.81 \approx 880 \text{ Pa}$, not the total of oil plus water.
options.C: This results from swapping the depths, using 5.0 cm for water and 9.0 cm for oil, which gives about $490 + 710 \approx 1200 \text{ Pa}$.
options.D: This is the sum of the oil pressure $\approx 390 \text{ Pa}$ and the water pressure $\approx 880 \text{ Pa}$, giving $\approx 1270 \text{ Pa} \approx 1300 \text{ Pa}$.
